newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP backs labelling rules for dangerous products.
newsitem.headline: EP backs labelling rules for dangerous products.

text.p: The European Parliament on Thursday approved plans to put clearer, more detailed warning labels on thousands of carcinogenic or poisonous substances and other dangerous products.

Over the years, the European Union has made numerous piecemeal attempts to standardise its member states' laws on classifying, packaging and labelling hazardous preparations, to ensure that users in all 15 EU countries receive equally detailed product safety information.
The result is a pile of different pieces of legislation, some relating to pure chemicals, others to preparations composed of two or more chemical substances, and a third set relating to pesticides.

Now the European Commission is proposing to bring all these laws together in a single binding directive, which will also update and extend the labelling requirements manufacturers will be obliged to fulfil.

Euro-MPs welcomed the draft directive, which will for the first time oblige manufacturers to put warning symbols on products which damage the environment and provide professional users with safety data for products which are not classed as dangerous -- because they contain only low concentrations of hazardous substances -- but which might be a health risk in use.
But parliament, which has joint say with EU ministers over environmental and consumer legislation, called for changes to strengthen the proposal.

The amendments may go some small way towards satisfying the three new EU countries -- Austria, Sweden and Finland -- which complain the new directive is not as stringent as their national laws and will force them to accept less well labelled products from other member states.

Euro-MPs said products should carry warning symbols when the cumulative total of a product's toxic, corrosive or otherwise dangerous ingredients exceeds a certain level, even when these substances do not individually reach that level.

The directive says product labels must carry not only danger symbols, including a tactile warning for blind people, but also the actual names of all substances which are toxic or cause cancer, mutations or allergies.
Parliament went even further and said labels should explicitly name individual corrosive, irritant and environmentally damaging substances.

But Euro-MPs did not call for labels which list every single hazardous detail of a product, on the grounds that this would confuse users and be too expensive for manufacturers forced to change their packaging -- a point stressed to parliament by EU Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann on Wednesday evening.

In addition to its demands on stricter labelling, parliament insisted that toxic products should only be tested on animals for the purpose of hazard classification if there is no alternative test method.
